of his old flair with a 37-point night: ‘It’s what I do’
 Trae Young and Kyshawn George celebrate after Young made a game-tying 3-pointer to force overtime on Thursday against the Detroit Pistons. Geoff Burke / Imagn Images 
 By Josh Robbins Nov. 13, 2026 Updated Share article 24 WASHINGTON — Fresh off another defeat, the Washington Wizards’ charter flight from Indianapolis International Airport to Dulles International Airport landed at approximately 12:45 Thursday morning.
 Less than 15 hours later, around 3:20 Thursday afternoon, Trae Young stood on the Capital One Arena court, launching shot after shot, hoping to regain the rhythm and groove that propelled him to four career All-Star nods but have been absent for much of the past three weeks.
 Advertisement
 Both Young and his Wizards teammates opened the day in the same predicament: wondering how a promising start to the 2026-27 season had turned sour so quickly, with five consecutive losses.
 On Thursday evening, against one of the Eastern Conference’s heavyweight clubs, the starting point guard and his teammates took a step toward finding their way again, losing in double overtime to the Detroit Pistons 144-140.
 “I’m just proud of the way we fought,” Young said. “We played to the end and battled.”
 Young scored 37 points and dished out 14 assists in a performance that also included a game-tying 3-pointer as time expired in the fourth quarter. It wasn’t a perfect night for him — he made only eight of the 23 shots he attempted from the field — but for one of the first times this season, he gave the Wizards hope that he can regain some of the scoring prowess he showed during his best years with the Atlanta Hawks.
 “Great growth by our team,” Wizards coach Brian Keefe said. “Trae Young was fantastic tonight leading us.”
 Alex Sarr also enjoyed a potential breakout night. Sarr has struggled to rediscover his offense this season when he has played alongside fellow big man Anthony Davis, but on Thursday, Sarr scored 30 points on 12-of-14 shooting against the Pistons, who continued to play without injured center Jalen Duren. Davis also had 30 points and added 15 rebounds.
 The Wizards start Sarr and Davis together when both of them are healthy, and for that lineup to make sense for the team’s half-court offense, Sarr needs to regain his long-range shooting stroke. Entering Thursday, he had made only seven of his 34 3-point tries this season, hurting the team’s spacing. Against the Pistons, though, he made four of the six treys he attempted.
 “I think I’m always confident shooting the ball,” Sarr said. “It either goes in or it doesn’t. We can build off a game like that, just for the whole team, just our effort, our energy. We had it down the stretch and we let it go. So it’s a lot of lessons to learn from that.”
 Advertisement
 The improved performance against the Pistons took place 24 hours after a 114-101 loss to the Indiana Pacers in which the Wizards’ offense often looked listless, with little player movement and ball movement. A lineup of Bub Carrington, Tre Johnson, Kyshawn George, Bilal Coulibaly and Sarr struggled during the opening minutes of the fourth quarter, allowing the Pacers to go on a 12-0 run to break the game open .
 Young’s play dipped during the team’s four-game road trip to Atlanta, Oklahoma City, Detroit and Indianapolis, intensifying questions about the wisdom of re-signing him to a four-year, $213 million contract during the offseason.
 On Thursday, both the offense and Young fared far better.
 Washington zipped the ball around the court for portions of the game, and Young took on a more aggressive posture, attacking often and drawing shooting fouls. He took 17 free throws and made all of them.
 “It’s what I do,” Young said. “I was never worried about it. I’m not fazed about what I’ve been doing early on in the season. I’m … more focused on our wins and losses, and for me, just putting ourselves in winning situations. And I don’t think I did a good enough job in the road games of putting us in winning situations.”
 Trae Young committed a shot-clock violation on the possession before his game-tying 3-pointer at the end of the fourth quarter. Geoff Burke / Imagn Images Young and the Wizards have a lot they need to work on. A case-in-point occurred after Cade Cunningham sank a pair of free throws to put the Pistons ahead 119-118 with 26.4 seconds remaining in the fourth quarter.
 Young brought the ball upcourt, and a screen by Davis forced defender extraordinaire Ausar Thompson to switch off guarding Young and forced Cunningham to guard Young. But Young could not take advantage of the matchup. Young twice fumbled his dribble, and by the time he launched a desperation shot from 22 feet, it was blocked by Cunningham, resulting in a shot-clock violation.
 Advertisement
 The Wizards fouled almost immediately, and Cunningham made both free throws, giving Detroit a 121-118 lead with 1.8 seconds remaining.
 Young caught the inbounds pass from George, pump-faked and made the shot from 29 feet to send the game into overtime.
 All those mid-afternoon shots had paid off.
 Young and his team now face difficult questions going forward. Can their offense retain the movement it produced against the defensive-minded Pistons? Will the team as a whole sustain its energy more consistently? And how can Young score more efficiently?
 It’s been a rough go so far. Young and his teammates hope that, even in a loss, Thursday provided a breakout moment. “If we continue to play like this, I can see ourselves winning a lot of games,” Young said.
